newsitem.title: UK: UK troops in Gulf were exposed to pesticide-paper.
newsitem.headline: UK troops in Gulf were exposed to pesticide-paper.

text.p: The government promised on Sunday to investigate claims that British soldiers in the 1991 Gulf War were not given protective clothing when spraying pesticides now suspected of causing so-called Gulf War Syndrome.
The Independent on Sunday newspaper, quoting restricted documents, said senior army officiers were repeatedly warned of the health risk but failed to provide protective equipment.

Defence Secretary Michael Portillo said the ministry, which admitted on Friday for the first time a possible line between organophosphate pesticides (OPs) and illnesses popularly known as Gulf War Syndrome, would carry out further investigations.
"Obviously we're talking about things that happened on the ground in a war situation," Portillo told Sky television.

"But clearly we must go back and find out whether people used these sprays, whether they were protected at the time, whether they should have been protected at the time -- these are all questions to be asked," he said.

There is no dispute that unusual numbers of Gulf War veterans have since been ill. But doctors disagree whether there is a consistent pattern to the ailments which should be classified as a "syndrome" and related to specific physical causes.

About 51,000 Britons were involved in the war against Iraq following Saddam Hussein's invasion of Kuwait. The government has refused to recognise a specific Gulf War Syndrome and has attributed any ailments to the stress of war.
But it has been investigating some 750 veterans suffering from chronic fatigue, asthma, depression and skin complaints.
Some veterans are now confined to wheelchairs and claim their children have suffered birth defects.

Richard Barr, a lawyer representing 400 Gulf War veterans, said one substance in the "cocktail" of immunisations soldiers were given to protect them against chemical and biological warfare magnified the effect of OPs by a factor of 10.

"We have spoken to a large number of troops, particulalry in connection with OPs, and all of them do confirm that, to put it very mildly, the safety arrangements were fairly slapdash," Barr told BBC radio.
The pesticides, some bought locally, were used to control insect-borne disease in the desert during the campaign.
In April, U.S. scientists said they had found that the combination of chemicals troops were exposed to in the Gulf had effects on animals similar to those experienced by veterans.
